analysis.one_liner: Gives workers 90 days' warning before large layoffs and extends health coverage for older displaced workers.
analysis.headline: The House committee passed the bill 26-18 in October 2007, but the full House never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen the federal WARN Act, which requires employers to warn workers before plant closings and mass layoffs. It extends the required warning from 60 to 90 days, covers layoffs of 25 or more workers at companies with 100 or more employees (a much lower threshold than current law), counts part-time workers, and lets the Labor Department investigate complaints and sue on workers' behalf. It also triples the maximum money penalty for skipping notice and extends COBRA health coverage for older or long-tenured workers certified as eligible for trade adjustment assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with 100 or more employees who face a closing or layoff affecting 25 or more people, including part-time workers who current law excludes. They would get three months' warning instead of two, information about unemployment and retraining benefits, a Labor Department complaint process, and higher payouts if the employer gives no notice. Workers 55 and older, or with 10 or more years on the job, whose layoff is certified as trade-related would keep buying COBRA health coverage beyond the normal 18-month limit.

how_it_helps.text: Requires 90 days' written notice before a plant closing or mass layoff, up from 60 days, and extends coverage to layoffs of 25 or more workers and to part-time employees.

Requires employers to tell affected workers what benefits are available — unemployment compensation, trade adjustment assistance, COBRA, and job-training services — and requires the Labor Department to notify the affected area's members of Congress.

Raises the penalty for inadequate notice to two days' pay per day short of the 90-day requirement, plus interest, and lets workers file complaints with the Labor Department, which can investigate with subpoena power and sue on their behalf.
Extends COBRA continuation health coverage beyond the normal period for workers 55 or older, or with 10 or more years of service, whose layoff is certified as trade-related.

Bars employers from making workers sign away their rights under the law in settlement agreements, except ones negotiated by the Labor Department, a state attorney general, or the worker's own attorney.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers — 100 or more employees — especially manufacturers and other firms with fluctuating workforces, who would face a longer warning period, liability for many more mid-size layoffs, part-time headcounts in the math, up to 180 days' pay per affected worker for skipping notice, and government enforcement on top of private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The new penalty formula (two days' pay for every day short of 90) can reach up to 180 days' pay per worker, triple the current-law maximum of back pay for each day of violation up to 60 days — a cost an honest supporter must acknowledge.

Lowering the coverage threshold to any layoff of 25 workers and counting part-time employees dramatically expands how many business decisions trigger the law, adding compliance costs for mid-size employers, not just the largest ones.
COBRA continuation coverage does not come with a subsidy — displaced workers pay the full group premium themselves, so extending the period mainly helps those who can afford steep monthly payments.
Department of Labor enforcement, complaint handling, and mandatory benefit guides would add federal administrative work and spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing a sudden layoff, an extra month of warning and a real enforcement mechanism are meaningful, and the benefit-information requirement addresses a genuine gap — many displaced workers never learn what aid exists. The costs fall on employers, chiefly larger ones in restructuring-heavy industries, and the tripled penalty and much lower coverage threshold would genuinely sting; whether the trade is worth it depends on how much weight one puts on predictability for workers versus flexibility for firms. The COBRA piece is the weakest part: extending the period without subsidizing premiums helps only those who can already pay.

outcome.mechanism: The committee passed it 26-18 and it was placed on the House calendar in October 2007, but House leadership never brought it to the floor, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA), chairman of the Education and Labor Committee, introduced the bill on October 10, 2007, with 13 Democratic cosponsors.
The committee considered and marked up the bill on October 18, 2007, and ordered it reported amended by a vote of 26 to 18.
The committee reported the amended bill on October 25, 2007 (H. Rept. 110-410), and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 258.
The bill never received a vote in the full House and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers kept the existing 60-day notice rule, the higher layoff thresholds, and the lighter penalties, with no new Labor Department enforcement; displaced workers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee's 26-18 vote was roughly along party lines in a Democratic-controlled committee, though the sources do not record each member's party.

industries.note: The bill triples the maximum layoff-notice penalty, extends the warning period to 90 days, and subjects many more mid-size layoffs — including part-time workers — to the law, with Labor Department enforcement added on top. Firms restructuring through layoffs would bear higher direct costs and less scheduling flexibility.

industries.industry: COBRA health plans and health insurers
industries.note: Extending COBRA eligibility for older or long-tenured trade-displaced workers adds premium-paying enrollees to group health plans. Workers pay the full premium themselves, so the industry gains customers without new cost to employers.
